review_text_raw:
I would prefer to give this game a 5/10, but unfortunately, that's not possible on Steam, so I’m rating it negatively for interested buyers to see.

I bought the game to unravel mysteries as an FBI operative—a game I could play for several hours. The gameplay mechanics are exactly what I was hoping for, but unfortunately, some of them are only used once throughout the entire game.
The story is extremely short, with a plot that becomes obvious within the first 40 minutes of gameplay. Seriously, 2 hours of gameplay for 14€? Not to meantion an "Original Soundtrack" for another 10€. If players could skip some dialogues and cutscenes, the game would only last 30 minutes. The story feels more like a detective TV show where everything is "weird," "doesn't make sense," and "everything is interconnected."

In summary:
+ The game mechanics are awesome! - Unfortunately, their potential is wasted on a simplistic story with a soap-opera-like plot seen more than thousands of times on TV.
+ The soundtrack (not bought), sound effects, and voice acting are excellent.
- The story is simple and feels rather sloppy (95% of the ideas went into coding and mechanics, 5% into the story). Perhaps it's due to the potential for a speedrunning community?
- When I calculate the "price per hour" of the main story, this game is undoubtedly the worst in my entire game library (7€ per hour (almost 12€ if you buy the "original soundtrack"), including cutscenes and dialogues).
- The game has unskippable cutscenes (returning home), dialogues (the tutorial), and end credits, likely so that you can’t get a refund within the 2-hour Steam policy.
? If the sequel to this game will also be only 2 hours long, the developers might as well not even bother. It’s not worth the money.

If the game was a bit longer (at least 4 hours of a decent story), I would recommend it, but unfortunately, I can't.
Definitely buy it during a sale, just not now.

Played the demo and got really hooked, so I bought the game the next day full price.

AFTER the demo I expected it to be very similar to Orville and Cyber Manhunt, with the primary focus on using the game's mechanics to solve multiple criminal cases, most unrelated or maybe filler and some interconnected into a bigger picture.
It was... kinda like that? But instead of a focus on multiple cases and the solving mechanics, it focuses solely on one storyline.

Which to me was actually really sad I guess because the gameplay mechanics were really well implemented and would have made for a super nice gameplay loop but instead got used once to advance the plot and then got discarded (e.g. the lab analysis or manually unlocking files). 

Also, the game is probably 75% dialogue, in which you are given choices that lead nowhere. You feel like your choices should matter, maybe in resulting in different endings but there is only one ending implemented. It actually made me compare it more to a visual novel than a detective game.

The lack of "filler cases" is also more of a negative in this particular storyline. I've read that the developer wanted to focus more on the main story instead of filler but I think some filler would've helped the player to immerse themselves better into their role, made better usage of the well-implemented mechanics and would've allowed the player to connect with the characters better, settle mentally on the twists and turns of the main story and process them before the next thing gets thrown at them. It felt very fast-paced with no breathing time from basically the get-go and if I'm not mistaken the story takes place within only a couple of days in-game which also does not seem realistic.

Conclusion:
+ well-made from a technical point of view
+ well implemented mechanics
+ good soundtrack
- poor use of mechanics
- unclear advertisement (detective game vs. very story-driven, more of a visual novel)
- no actual choices made by the player even though it feels like they should have mattered
- lack of cases with a rather short gameplay time as a result
- lots of dialogue with comparatively little gameplay

If you're looking for somethin akin to Orville, Cyber Manhunt or even Her Story, this is not it.
I considered requesting a refund but I believe that if I buy a product, receive it and use it, there is no reason in refunding it, even if it was not what I expected

The game has a great concept and some thrilling moments. The developers did a fantastic job immersing you in the feeling of being a "cog in a machine". The music, interface design, story theme, and execution were excellent. I especially enjoyed the quiet moments where I could read through various documents and explore the backstory and world the developers created.

That’s why it pains me so much that all this hard work feels utterly underutilized. You’re essentially handheld and dragged through a linear story, with little to no impact from your choices. There are intricate mechanics that seem fun once you struggle through their first use, but they are never used again. It is just a little bit more "game" than a "interactive movie".

I don’t want to be cruel—I can see the developers put a lot of effort into it—but it was just far too short.

EDIT: I've been thinking about this a lot, and I just wanted to add one more thing. You can see how I go into quite a bit of initial, just-coming-down-off-finishing-the-game detail down below if you'd like, but I'd like to quickly say here, at the start, that I think a big part of the issue was a fundamental misunderstanding of what this game was. I went into this expecting a puzzle game, but it isn't so much a puzzle game as it is a story game.
I feel it's advertised as more of a puzzle game with subtle hints at an overarching story you might be able to uncover, and indeed it does *play* like a puzzle game... until it very much becomes about following the narrative.
My feelings below still stand - including the ones after my spoiler tags - but while I don't know that I would've felt *differently* if I'd gone into this expecting something different, much of my confusion and disappointment might've been at least softened.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Overall, I was pretty disappointed with this game.
First, it was incredibly short - I had the game open for 7-ish hours... but I had dinner, fed the dogs, took a shower, yada yada, with it paused, so I'm not actually sure how long it really took. Most of the puzzles themselves weren't particularly challenging - though the mechanics were satisfying in a point-and-click, ASMR kind of way - and then one or two of the puzzles were SUPER, out-of-pocket complicated, insanely difficult, and totally out of place?? And because of the length of the game, I felt like all the mechanics I was learning, I really didn't need for very long, or often even more than once.
The writing, acting, sound design, and off-screen auditory storytelling were beautiful. Very well done; you can tell a lot of love went into it, there just... wasn't a whole lot of content.

I saw someone mention that if there were an "operator mode," that would make up for a lot of this problem, and I agree. *MILD SPOILER* Every single one of the cases were directly linked to the main story, and I think being able to enjoy some of the mechanics for longer would make it feel a little more worthwhile. Again, many of the puzzles were fairly simple, but it was still fun and satisfying in a way, and then it would also be more impactful - learning how to do the more complicated puzzles - because you'd have to use that knowledge again.

**SPOILERS FOR THE END**

The ending was incredibly dissatisfying to me. I immediately got off and looked to see if I somehow got "the bad ending" and there was another way I could've played to get "the good ending," but no. It is what it is - one and done. (I saw someone else say that if there HAD been multiple endings, that would also help with the overarching "the game is too short" issue everyone seems to be having, and I agree with that, as well.)
Some people liked the ending, but a lot of people shared the same feelings I have: if I uncover the mystery, am taking notes on the story and correctly piecing together the clues, I want to feel like I 'won' the video game... at least to a degree. But (again, **HUGE SPOILER AHEAD**) it literally doesn't matter at all. Nothing you did, none of the choices you made, mattered. The main character you played dies, every SINGLE one of your contacts/friends dies or goes missing (you cannot save them, it does not matter, and you're informed of their demise in during-credits news clippings, no less), and the only one to escape is HAL, and they're still trying to take down the big bad 30 years later (which is what fans of the ending consider the "silver lining.")
I love when games do some out-of-the-box stuff, but the whole game sets you up like you're uncovering a mystery, exposing a story, and then in the end literally not a lick of it mattered (except that HAL escaped and is still trying, which as far as I can tell, happens no matter what you, as the player, do.) It just felt very forced, and pretty pointless.
Disappointing, because again, some of the mechanics were really neat, and you can tell a lot of love was put into the storytelling aspects.

I had fun. I also almost requested a refund after finishing it because the ending made me so angry. [spoiler]It's not a happy ending, which is fine, but it's also not a satisfying ending. Choices are ultimately meaningless because an apparently superhuman hitman escapes custody in a high-security building (the story even makes a point of saying how secure this building is when you're helping another character find the passkey for the locker room) and is then apparently omniscient as he knows exactly where to find the director of this highly secure organization during a security lockdown, exactly when to intercept to main character en route to the exit, and is then able to ascend from the parking garage to the eighth floor to eliminate the supervisor/insider contact of our benevolent hacker companion all apparently without facing the slightest resistance from security in what is basically this universe's FBI HQ. Did the mole have him memorize the layout of the entire building? For what reason? After all that you're treated to a series of newspaper headlines letting you know that absolutely every ally you had over the course of the game is either dead, imprisoned, or missing. All tension goes out the window and it just turns into a cascade of tragedy for no clear reason. It's just so unbelievable to me. Maybe if it was clear from the start that this was more like a part 1 to a larger story or something, I would be more forgiving, but I expected a satisfying conclusion when I bought the game. Not super-hitman destroys everything because *dismissive raspberry sounds*[/spoiler]

With all that said, I do think the developer has a lot of potential. The puzzles were interesting and solving them felt really satisfying.

The game really was not what I expected. From the store page, I thought it would be fairly puzzle focused, with a lot of scanning evidence and connecting dots. But in reality, it plays out more like a visual novel with some very simple puzzles thrown in. There were multiple elements that seemed like they would be recurring features, but were used a single time and never again. Many pieces of evidence are teased, but are never actually shown before the game ends. The game feels like it ends *way* too quickly. It took me just over three hours to finish. I'm fine with shorter games, but there's so much potential here that goes nowhere because the game ends so soon.

On the plus side, the presentation is great. Despite mostly being a computer screen, the visuals have a certain flare to them that leans into the setting. The soundtrack compliments the narrative at every step, swelling at big reveals and calming down after tense moments. And the voice actors give solid performances. No complaints on this aspect.

As for the narrative, it's fairly compelling. You can definitely see a lot of the twists coming before they happen, but the presentation makes it interesting to see play out regardless. That being said, it again suffers from being too short. You're meant to be unraveling a big conspiracy over the course of the game, but by the time it's over, it feels like you've barely stuck your toes in. I was invested in what was happening, had just had a big reveal, and then... suddenly the credits are rolling.

There are definitely things to like about this game, but I have a hard time recommending it, especially if your mostly here for that "Investigation" tag. It's too short, too easy, and doesn't quite live up to what it says on the box. It feels like a demo for a larger game, but I kind of just wanted the larger game to begin with.

Some interesting concepts and a fun story. Cool twist too. Most of the puzzles were relatively straightforward, but the "manual reading" one was actually pretty exciting and interesting, and the "identifying the feed" one was clever. I just could not get past the ridiculous anachronisms popping up constantly, and some very confusing internal logic.

This game takes place in 1992. Everybody has a cell phone, digital photography is commonly accessible, "zoom, enhance" is an actual mechanic. The game's FBI analogue has a database with facial recognition data of nearly everyone in the country? In 1992??? In 2025 sure, but not in 1992. Agents are constantly uploading files to your computer from their phone. At one point, confusingly, an agent apparently sends you physical floppy disks.... via his phone...? Baffling honestly. I was willing to set aside the fact that VoIP didn't exist in 1992 either, but after a while you simply cannot suspend your disbelief any further. 

HAL's "hacking" capabilities are completely inconsistent, and the justifications for why they can't hack a particular thing make no narrative sense a lot of the time. Credit where credit's due though, nothing stands out to me as anachronistic about HAL's methods at least.

There's a big narrative-UX disconnect as well. Initially I thought the "phone calls" you receive from agents are just game objects showing transcripts of audio conversations, but at one point you're instructed to *enter a code into the chat box* as though it were a terminal. So now I'm asked to believe that my computer has been *actually transcribing* phone calls automatically while people are speaking to me, and that I can use this function as a terminal. Completely ridiculous. 

This game would have made way more sense if it were set in the current year, with minimal changes to the story or mechanics, but I think the devs were just too enamoured with the retro aesthetic to let it go so they set it in the 90s anyways. 

Side note: I had annoying bug where my keybinds weren't showing up in-game, so anything where I was required to press a key just had [???] instead. Not game breaking, just annoying.

This game has so much going on that I would ideally like to praise but a lot of those same things are also why I didn't really enjoy it.  On the bright side it has a very clever user interface system I like where most of the game is controlled via a "computer", the puzzles range from really easy to more complicated, and the story has some creativity going on.  It's definitely somewhat interesting, very dialogue heavy, and I would not recommend if you're not a strong reader, lover of puzzle games, or if you like a lot of scenery or environment changes.

With that said, the user interface becomes tiring to interact with very quickly.  It's hard to convey a sense of importance or immediate action when most of the puzzles really come down to clicking and having a computer "analyze" random clues. review_text_raw:
This game only has one ending, and only less than 2½ - 3 hours of content in total, making the cost per played hour very high. 
The one singular ending is quite bad, and even though there are many dialogue options, there are no actual meaningful choices to be made.
There are numerous quite long and somewhat boring unskippable cut scenes. However one could argue that having no skip option is acceptable due to it being somewhat important to pay attention to the them. And since there's only one ending, there's no replayability, and so there's no need to have a skip option. Though realistically, and as others have pointed out, the most probable reason for not having a skip option is to extend the required playtime to over 2 hours so the game cannot be refunded through Steam.
The game has a lot of dialogue, and not a lot of gameplay. What little actual gameplay there is, is enjoyable enough I guess, but also pretty simplistic and easy. This can be seen as both a positive and a negative. If you're looking for any sort of a challenge/puzzle, you will not find it in this game. This game should be definitely thought of as a visual novel more than a puzzle game.
The story itself is mediocre and actually pretty shallow, which is very bad for a game that consists mainly of the story.
The dialogue is fully voice-acted (except for [spoiler]HAL[/spoiler] and the protagonist), which is a definite plus. The voice acting is also pretty high-quality. However I cannot help but feel like way too much developer effort and money was put into the voice acting, when it should've been put into other aspects of the game.
The soundscape and the soundtrack are also good, but really nothing out of the ordinary.

Overall, The Operator is a short, pricey mediocre dialogue-heavy and minimal-gameplay game with high-quality voice acting and heavy hand-holding and railroading, and with only one ending. It feels like the game was designed to be just long enough to make it impossible to refund after reaching the ending (which in fairness one shouldn't do regardless, if they enjoyed the game and reached the ending).

I cannot recommend anything else but to watch someone else such as a YouTuber play this game. I think that will actually add way more to the experience than buying the game and playing it on your own.

review_text_raw:
This game has an interesting premise and it has been made well. The graphics are good and the audio is top notch in my books.

But unfortunately it's... hmm, how should I say it... easy? Or not even that, hand-heldy! Like, it doesn't really let you do much anything of worth outside of one high stakes scene that is timed. But that it not what 99% of the game is.

It's kinda like this game is backwards from what you would expect from a logic puzzle game. It's the Agents or other people that call you aka the NPC's aka the game itself that do most of the detective work. And you, the player, are the computer whose job is to do the tedious work of checking. You get one single question to answer from the field agent and the answer is never that hard to find. In fact it's almost never necessary to collect and compile information as an active researcher and there's basically no need to take notes. Most of the times you just click on the right, kinda obvious document and do the thing and then answer so the plot may thiccen.

And it's not like the setting of the game, you being the computer guy helping detectives in the field means it has to be boring. There could have been more you could do. But most of the intrigue in this game comes from chat interactions, not from actual action you get to do.

Like for example, there are two things that could have been so fun to get to use as active participant, as part of a larger puzzle YOU need to solve yourself, the chemical analysis software and the bomb defusing manual, that only get one use. And also, no love for the vehicle database, just for people database. But like, just being able to do more than to just find out an answer to one question at a time, being able to take notes and to make actual deductions? Would have been fun. Think of Mainlining as an example.

It's just that, there is so much promise. This game was instant purchase for me as soon as I found out about it, as a fan of mystery and "hacking" genre of games. But it just didn't really deliver what I hoped for. And I'm kinda bummed about it.

It's an interesting game and I enjoyed playing a bit of it, but the developer has a specific idea in mind about how it is to be played and I'm not into that.  Specifically, when listening to an audio file, the controls are locked and you can't do anything else.  The developer has said that he wants to be able to focus the player's attention, but that's not how my attention works and it's very uncomfortable.  Instead of focusing my intention, it's like someone powered up a megaphone next to my ear and is shouting, "this is all artificial!  Stop being immersed!  This is a video game!  The stakes are very low because none of this is real!"

The ideal situation for me would be being able to replay all of the audios - including recordings of the "real time" conversations - repeatedly while I peruse the visual and text data.  This is how I have investigated things in the past (though those were technical investigations and not criminal investigations): get everything in front of me and let my mind chew on a bunch of it at once to get into it.

I'm not exactly normal when it comes to my focus and attention, but the make or break question for Steam reviews is, "would I recommend this?"  In this case, I don't.

UPDATE: I'm not suggesting that the dev should change the game to suit me; I'm just saying that I don't recommend it.

review_text_raw:
I almost never leave reviews, so bear with me.

I was kind of enthralled by the demo: I loved the idea of drawing connections, of looking something up in one database and comparing it to the next database and finding it on a list retrieved earlier.  Then...well, I'm [i]not[/i] going to say is "bait and switch"; I think the demo is a fair representation of the game.  But the game did go in different directions than I'd hoped: for instance, the connection-drawing is in many ways the core of the game, but there was a lot of stuff around it: dialogue choices, minigames  ("oh, look, mastermind"), occasional long cutscenes.

At its core the game is a thriller, which is not really my genre.  (There's literally a "Them", which I think is the same as "The Organization", which is what you get if you ask LLMs to summarize the thriller genre.)  I could have guessed that, probably, but there's so much that seems to pay homage to [i]The X-Files[/i] (the FBI in the 1990s, the typewritten location captions, your boss is literally named Skinner for heaven's sake), and one of the first cases you get is alien-abduction-based.  This ended up being way more "thriller" in tone than X-Files was.

But to be clear: I didn't hate it!  I wish Steam had a scale more subtle than "yes/no", because I want to give it a "qualified yes" or maybe a "no, but if it's your thing, then yes".  There's a lot to like here: the atmosphere (even if you could practically see the words "cue dramatic music" at major plot twists), the interface, even a lot of the writing and plot.  Much of the voice acting is good; I really liked Pendell and Walker; Andrews less so.  (The two coroner reports, even less.)  And the [spoiler]bomb-defusing scene[/spoiler] did a great job with the tone.

Ultimately, I don't [i]regret[/i] playing it.  I also just don't recommend it unless you're looking for a thriller.  In which case, enjoy!

review_text_raw:
I can't really recommend this game for the price being asked.

The Operator has a lot of good things going for it, the premise and story are interesting and the puzzle gameplay keeps itself fresh so nothing feels tedious. Special mention must be made about the high quality of the sound design - both the voice acting and the choice and timing of the music stings are excellent.

The biggest problem with The Operator for me is that it all falls apart just as it was gaining momentum. The last set of puzzles lack the sense of discovery from earlier, the game abruptly ends leaving a bunch of unanswered questions, and you're left feeling like nothing you did mattered.

This feels like the kind of game that should have multiple endings or changes caused by the player decisions, but there is nothing like that here. This is a specific story that you're being taken on a ride for - one with a pretty obvious "twist" - and no replayability.

If this was a prologue or chapter one of a larger game I would feel more favourable to this, but in its current state I wouldn't recommend this unless it's at least half price.

I have to say I was absolutely hooked with the concept of [i] The Operator. [/i] One watch of the trailer will tell you why; an operator helping with government investigations, analyzing clues, basically being the man-in-the-chair? It's all awesome! But what killed the mood for me was the cliche writing, amateur voice acting, and the simplistic puzzles. First of all the writing. Who TALKS like this?! Every person you meet is quippy, chippy, or clever with their line delivery. These don't sound like professional field agents, they sound like cartoon characters. A man has been killed, TAKE THIS SERIOUSLY! They should be more realistic, a bit grittier, more direct. And why am I doing everything? What exactly is your job here??

Next are the puzzles. They are already simple enough, but I feel babied and talked down to by the characters we meet. The game would make itself so much more compelling if there were harder applications! Something I had to grill through to find what my agent needed. So far, I can click two buttons and get the answer to the riddle. I don't [i] feel [/i] like a secret agent, which is what I bought the game for. And not to mention the game's animations for security footage, which are taken so seriously for how poor in quality they are. The tone simply doesn't match. 

Finally, I had a sincerely hard time caring about the story of the game. The plot was mildly interesting, conspiracies and hackers and whatnot, but it didn't land. Mainly because it meant wading through monologues from the characters, which drove me insane. If the game was harder, there would be much more to invest in. I would feel accomplished! But after completing the first two days, I feel like there was no other option but to succeed. There was never any risk of me failing, which made it hard for me to connect to the game at all. In the end it was not the experience I was expecting, and if you're looking to be a tech-savvy sleuth, look elsewhere.

The Operator feels more like a short demo than a full game. The entire experience is over in just a few hours, making it hard to justify the full price—definitely one to buy only at a discount.

The game revolves around solving a single case from start to finish. While that might sound intriguing, it quickly becomes clear that they could have added a few standalone missions beforehand to build up engagement. Instead, you’re thrown into one investigation with no variety.

The tools available for solving the case are extremely limited. Some mechanics feel underdeveloped, and many tools are used only once, making them feel pointless rather than integral to the gameplay.

Overall, The Operator is a bland and forgettable experience. It lacks depth, variety, and replay value, making it hard to recommend.

So I feel VERY conflicted on this one.  95% of this game is marvelous and I totally recommend it to people who like figuring things out.  The 5% is so disappointing that I'm near dumbfounded.

The voice acting was more on the "okay but could be better" side of things (specifically Skinner, dude sounded like a robot). 
Now the bad.  Sorry for the spoilers, but the end is just so bad.  The between shift cutscenes (if you call super blurred nonsense a cutscene) were a total waste other than to give a sound cue to solve an end game puzzle and to make the answer to that puzzle not immediately obvious. I dunno if they were going for dark and edgy or if they wanted something that would happen in real life, but either way I play games for the illusion that good guys can win. review_text_raw:
Game has good base features, such as databases and interactable video/image search functions, as well as references to certain lab and analysis tools. There was also good voice acting and character designs.
However, I had not realized game was such a railroaded linear story line with no real choices or variation in gameplay. Several points where game takes control from player and forces unnecessary video or audio cutscenes that do not add well to the experience or even the story. Certain events forcibly squish the interactable area of the screen, making it difficult to maneuver through the various game elements needed to continue. Not friendly to slow readers, as whenever a new line of text appears, it forces the log to the bottom, forcing you to wait until the whole conversation is over to double check the one thing you wanted to check in the conversation, such as spelling of a name you want to look up.
Would not recommend for anything more than $4.99

A very nice but short puzzle-solving visual novel. The writing was enjoyable and the soundtrack is top-notch. The puzzle-solving may not be entirely intuitive at first glance, but the atmosphere of being pulled out of your element at times definitely comes into play.

And it collapses on itself in the end. The suspension of disbelief the writing begs you to undertake to believe that what happened is in any way reasonable to the story's narrative up unto that point is so massive that I wouldn't shoulder it even if I could.
